claim: During clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) in eukaryotes, actin assembly is required to overcome large membrane tension and turgor pressure.
source: During clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) in eukaryotes, actin assembly is required to overcome large membrane tension and turgor pressure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and is consistent with established scientific knowledge about CME.

claim: The molecular mechanisms by which the actin machinery adapts to varying membrane tension remain unknown.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms by which the actin machinery adapts to varying membrane tension remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, indicating a gap in understanding.

claim: How cells reduce their membrane tension when they are challenged by hypotonic shocks remains unclear.
source: In addition, how cells reduce their membrane tension when they are challenged by hypotonic shocks remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, indicating a gap in understanding.

claim: Cells rapidly reduce their membrane tension using three parallel mechanisms.
source: We used quantitative microscopy to demonstrate that cells rapidly reduce their membrane tension using three parallel mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript using quantitative microscopy.

claim: Yeast cells use their cell wall for mechanical protection.
source: In addition to using their cell wall for mechanical protection, yeast cells disassemble eisosomes to buffer moderate changes in membrane tension on a minute time scale.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing walled cells and protoplasts.

claim: Yeast cells disassemble eisosomes to buffer moderate changes in membrane tension on a minute time scale.
source: In addition to using their cell wall for mechanical protection, yeast cells disassemble eisosomes to buffer moderate changes in membrane tension on a minute time scale.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing eisosome disassembly after hypotonic shocks (Figure 1H and I).

claim: A temporary reduction in the rate of endocytosis for 2–6 min after hypotonic shock allows cells to add large pools of membrane to the plasma membrane.
source: Meanwhile, a temporary reduction in the rate of endocytosis for 2–6 min and an increase in the rate of exocytosis for at least 5 min allow cells to add large pools of membrane to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring endocytosis rates after hypotonic shocks (Figure 3).

claim: An increase in the rate of exocytosis for at least 5 min after hypotonic shock allows cells to add large pools of membrane to the plasma membrane.
source: Meanwhile, a temporary reduction in the rate of endocytosis for 2–6 min and an increase in the rate of exocytosis for at least 5 min allow cells to add large pools of membrane to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring exocytosis rates after hypotonic shocks (Figure 4).

claim: The endocytic actin machinery of fission yeast cells rapidly adapts to perform CME after abrupt increases in membrane tension.
source: We built on these results to submit the cells to abrupt increases in membrane tension and determine that the endocytic actin machinery of fission yeast cells rapidly adapts to perform CME.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing actin dynamics after hypotonic shocks (Figure 7).

claim: The internal turgor pressure of Saccharomyces cerevisiae is approximately 0.6 MPa.
source: In yeast cells, these resisting forces are particularly large because their internal turgor pressure is high, ranging from ~0.6 MPa for Saccharomyces cerevisiae to more than 1 MPa for Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Davì et al., 2018; Minc et al., 2009; Schaber et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that measured turgor pressure.

claim: The internal turgor pressure of Schizosaccharomyces pombe is more than 1 MPa.
source: In yeast cells, these resisting forces are particularly large because their internal turgor pressure is high, ranging from ~0.6 MPa for Saccharomyces cerevisiae to more than 1 MPa for Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Davì et al., 2018; Minc et al., 2009; Schaber et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that measured turgor pressure.

claim: The formation of an endocytic vesicle requires several thousands of piconewtons (pN).
source: Consequently, the formation of a vesicle requires several thousands of piconewtons (pN) (Dmitrieff and Nédélec, 2015; Ma and Berro, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that calculated the forces required for vesicle formation.

claim: Actin dynamics is required for productive endocytosis in yeast.
source: Previous studies have shown that actin dynamics is required for productive endocytosis in yeast (Aghamohammadzadeh et al., 2014; Basu et al., 2014; Carlsson and Bayly, 2014; Palmer et al., 2015) and in mammalian cells when membrane tension is high (Aghamohammadzadeh and Ayscough, 2009; Boulant et al., 2011; Hassinger et al., 2017), or when membrane scission proteins are absent (Ferguson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Actin dynamics is required for productive endocytosis in mammalian cells when membrane tension is high.
source: Previous studies have shown that actin dynamics is required for productive endocytosis in yeast (Aghamohammadzadeh et al., 2014; Basu et al., 2014; Carlsson and Bayly, 2014; Palmer et al., 2015) and in mammalian cells when membrane tension is high (Aghamohammadzadeh and Ayscough, 2009; Boulant et al., 2011; Hassinger et al., 2017), or when membrane scission proteins are absent (Ferguson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Actin dynamics is required for productive endocytosis in mammalian cells when membrane scission proteins are absent.
source: Previous studies have shown that actin dynamics is required for productive endocytosis in yeast (Aghamohammadzadeh et al., 2014; Basu et al., 2014; Carlsson and Bayly, 2014; Palmer et al., 2015) and in mammalian cells when membrane tension is high (Aghamohammadzadeh and Ayscough, 2009; Boulant et al., 2011; Hassinger et al., 2017), or when membrane scission proteins are absent (Ferguson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Actin assembly at the endocytic site is believed to provide the forces that overcome turgor pressure and membrane tension to deform the plasma membrane.
source: Actin assembly at the endocytic site is believed to provide the forces that overcome turgor pressure and membrane tension to deform the plasma membrane, but the precise mechanisms of force production remain unknown (reviewed in Berro and Lacy, 2018; Goode et al., 2015; Lacy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The precise mechanisms of force production during CME remain unknown.
source: Actin assembly at the endocytic site is believed to provide the forces that overcome turgor pressure and membrane tension to deform the plasma membrane, but the precise mechanisms of force production remain unknown (reviewed in Berro and Lacy, 2018; Goode et al., 2015; Lacy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The yeast cell wall has a high stiffness of approximately 50 MPa.
source: The yeast cell wall is believed to buffer abrupt changes in turgor pressure, thanks to its high stiffness of ~50 MPa (Atilgan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Yeast eisosomes can disassemble when cells without a cell wall (protoplasts) are placed in low osmolarity media.
source: In addition, similarly to mammalian cells' caveolae, which change shape or disassemble in response to increased membrane tension, yeast eisosomes can also disassemble when cells without a cell wall, called protoplasts, are placed in low osmolarity media (Kabeche et al., 2015; Parton et al., 2020; Sinha et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It remains unknown how eisosomes may regulate plasma membrane tension in intact cells.
source: However, it remains unknown how eisosomes may regulate plasma membrane tension in intact cells and whether eisosome disassembly directly influences cellular processes such as CME.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It remains unknown whether eisosome disassembly directly influences cellular processes such as CME.
source: However, it remains unknown how eisosomes may regulate plasma membrane tension in intact cells and whether eisosome disassembly directly influences cellular processes such as CME.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It remains unclear to which extent endocytosis and exocytosis may contribute to the regulation of membrane tension when cells are challenged with an abrupt increase in membrane tension.
source: In addition, it remains unclear to which extent endocytosis and exocytosis may contribute to the regulation of membrane tension when the cells are challenged with an abrupt increase in membrane tension.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Fission yeast is an ideal model system to quantitatively study the regulation mechanisms of membrane tension and its influence on the endocytic machinery.
source: Fission yeast is an ideal model system to quantitatively study the regulation mechanisms of membrane tension and its influence on the endocytic machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by reasoning about the properties of fission yeast as a model system.

claim: Yeast turgor pressure is high, so actin is required for CME in yeast.
source: First, because yeast turgor pressure is high, actin is required for CME.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the high turgor pressure in yeast.

claim: Yeast cells are devoid of any adhesion machinery or actin cortex.
source: Second, contrary to mammalian cells, yeast cells are devoid of any adhesion machinery or actin cortex, which usually complicates membrane tension manipulation and result interpretation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about yeast cell biology.

claim: Eisosomes in protoplasts at steady state in 1.2 M sorbitol are qualitatively similar to those in walled cells.
source: Our data show that eisosomes in protoplasts at steady state in 1.2 M sorbitol are qualitatively similar to those in walled cells (Figure 1A), and the cellular concentration of Pi1lp is the same in both conditions (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and 1E.

claim: The cellular concentration of Pil1p is the same in walled cells and protoplasts at steady state in 1.2 M sorbitol.
source: Our data show that eisosomes in protoplasts at steady state in 1.2 M sorbitol are qualitatively similar to those in walled cells (Figure 1A), and the cellular concentration of Pi1lp is the same in both conditions (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The surface area of the protoplasts' plasma membrane covered by eisosomes decreased with decreasing media osmolarity at steady state.
source: However, the surface area of the protoplasts' plasma membrane covered by eisosomes decreased with decreasing media osmolarity at steady state (Figure 1B and C) and correlated with increasing cell volume (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, 1C, and 1D.

claim: The surface area of the protoplasts' plasma membrane covered by eisosomes correlated with increasing cell volume.
source: However, the surface area of the protoplasts' plasma membrane covered by eisosomes decreased with decreasing media osmolarity at steady state (Figure 1B and C) and correlated with increasing cell volume (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Eisosomes disassembled rapidly after a hypotonic shock, dropping to approximately 50% of the surface area covered by eisosomes before the shock within 5 min.
source: Eisosomes disassembled rapidly after the hypotonic shock, dropping to ~50% of the surface area covered by eisosomes before the shock within 5 min, indicating a fast response to counteract the hypotonic shock and an eventual change in membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: At steady state in 0.8 M sorbitol, the membrane tension was 0.45 ± 0.14 mN·m−1 for wild-type protoplasts.
source: At steady state in 0.8 M sorbitol, the membrane tension was 0.45 ± 0.14 mN·m−1 for wild-type (WT) protoplasts and 0.39 ± 0.13 mN·m−1 for pil1Δ protoplasts (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: At steady state in 0.8 M sorbitol, the membrane tension was 0.39 ± 0.13 mN·m−1 for pil1Δ protoplasts.
source: At steady state in 0.8 M sorbitol, the membrane tension was 0.45 ± 0.14 mN·m−1 for wild-type (WT) protoplasts and 0.39 ± 0.13 mN·m−1 for pil1Δ protoplasts (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Within 5 min after a hypotonic shock of ΔC = −0.2 M, membrane tension increased 1.6-fold for wild-type protoplasts (0.73 ± 0.21 mN·m−1).
source: We then repeated these measurements within 5 min after inducing a hypotonic shock of ΔC = −0.2 M. We observed a 1.6-fold increase in membrane tension for WT protoplasts (0.73 ± 0.21 mN·m−1) and a 4.5-fold increase for protoplasts lacking eisosomes (1.74 ± 0.61 mN·m−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Within 5 min after a hypotonic shock of ΔC = −0.2 M, membrane tension increased 4.5-fold for protoplasts lacking eisosomes (1.74 ± 0.61 mN·m−1).
source: We then repeated these measurements within 5 min after inducing a hypotonic shock of ΔC = −0.2 M. We observed a 1.6-fold increase in membrane tension for WT protoplasts (0.73 ± 0.21 mN·m−1) and a 4.5-fold increase for protoplasts lacking eisosomes (1.74 ± 0.61 mN·m−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Eisosomes participate in the adjustment of plasma membrane tension.
source: This result demonstrates that eisosomes participate in the adjustment of plasma membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the membrane tension measurements showing different responses in wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts.

claim: Wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts initially at steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol survived small hypotonic shocks (ΔC = 0.05 M) equally well.
source: WT and pil1Δ protoplasts initially at steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol survived small hypotonic shocks (ΔC = 0.05 M) equally well (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: pil1Δ protoplasts were more sensitive to moderate hypotonic shocks (ΔC = 0.1 M) than wild-type protoplasts.
source: However, pil1Δ protoplasts were more sensitive to moderate hypotonic shocks (ΔC = 0.1 M) since most of them were unable to survive 2 min after the moderate shock while virtually all the WT protoplasts were able to survive (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Eisosomes protect protoplasts from changes in their membrane tension, but only to a small extent.
source: Altogether, these experiments demonstrate that (a) eisosomes protect protoplasts from changes in their membrane tension, but only to a small extent, and (b) without eisosomes, protoplasts can withstand only minor increase in their membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the survival data of wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts after hypotonic shocks.

claim: Without eisosomes, protoplasts can withstand only minor increase in their membrane tension.
source: Altogether, these experiments demonstrate that (a) eisosomes protect protoplasts from changes in their membrane tension, but only to a small extent, and (b) without eisosomes, protoplasts can withstand only minor increase in their membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the survival data of pil1Δ protoplasts after hypotonic shocks.

claim: Both wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells can survive a single osmotic shock of ΔC = −1.2 M.
source: In contrast, we found that both wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells can survive a single osmotic shock of ΔC = −1.2 M, which initially led us to think that eisosomes only have a minor protective role in walled cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Subsequent osmotic shocks led to a higher mortality of pil1Δ compared to wild-type walled cells.
source: However, we noticed that subsequent osmotic shocks led to a higher mortality of pil1Δ compared to wild-type walled cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Almost all wild-type walled cells remained alive after several osmotic shocks.
source: While almost all the wild-type walled cells remained alive after several shocks, around 10% of pil1Δ walled cells died after each subsequent shock (Figure 2E, F and G; supplementary video 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E, F, and G.

claim: Around 10% of pil1Δ walled cells died after each subsequent osmotic shock.
source: While almost all the wild-type walled cells remained alive after several shocks, around 10% of pil1Δ walled cells died after each subsequent shock (Figure 2E, F and G; supplementary video 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E, F, and G.

claim: Even in walled cells, eisosomes exert a protective role, likely by buffering sudden changes in membrane tension.
source: These results demonstrate that, even in walled cells, eisosomes exert a protective role, likely by buffering sudden changes in membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the survival data of wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells after repeated osmotic shocks.

claim: Within a few minutes of a hypotonic shock, the volume of wild-type protoplasts increased up to 50%.
source: Within a few minutes of a hypotonic shock, the volume of WT protoplasts increased up to 50% and the volume of pil1Δ protoplasts increased up to 20% (Figure 3A and B, insets).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A inset.

claim: Within a few minutes of a hypotonic shock, the volume of pil1Δ protoplasts increased up to 20%.
source: Within a few minutes of a hypotonic shock, the volume of WT protoplasts increased up to 50% and the volume of pil1Δ protoplasts increased up to 20% (Figure 3A and B, insets).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B inset.

claim: Total eisosome disassembly could release about 5% of the total surface area of the plasma membrane.
source: However, the corresponding increase in surface area cannot be explained by eisosome disassembly alone – total eisosome disassembly could release about 5% of the total surface area of the plasma membrane, assuming eisosomes are hemi-cylinders with a diameter of ~50 nm and cells contain 1.6 μm of eisosomes per μm2 of plasma membrane on average (Kabeche et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on calculations using assumptions about eisosome geometry and density, with a citation to previous work.

claim: For all shocks tested in wild-type protoplasts (ΔC = −0.05, −0.1, and −0.2 M), the endocytic density significantly decreased immediately after the hypotonic shock.
source: For all shocks tested in wild-type (ΔC = −0.05, −0.1, and −0.2 M) and pil1Δ protoplasts (ΔC = −0.025, −0.05, and −0.1 M) initially at steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol, the endocytic density in protoplasts significantly decreased immediately after the hypotonic shock (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For all shocks tested in pil1Δ protoplasts (ΔC = −0.025, −0.05, and −0.1 M), the endocytic density significantly decreased immediately after the hypotonic shock.
source: For all shocks tested in wild-type (ΔC = −0.05, −0.1, and −0.2 M) and pil1Δ protoplasts (ΔC = −0.025, −0.05, and −0.1 M) initially at steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol, the endocytic density in protoplasts significantly decreased immediately after the hypotonic shock (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The decrease in endocytic density increased with increasing hypotonic shocks, up to 36% for wild-type protoplasts after a ΔC = −0.2 M shock.
source: The difference increased with increasing hypotonic shocks, up to 36% for wild-type protoplasts after a ΔC = −0.2 M shock, and 79% for pil1Δ protoplasts after a ΔC = −0.1 M shock (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The decrease in endocytic density increased with increasing hypotonic shocks, up to 79% for pil1Δ protoplasts after a ΔC = −0.1 M shock.
source: The difference increased with increasing hypotonic shocks, up to 36% for wild-type protoplasts after a ΔC = −0.2 M shock, and 79% for pil1Δ protoplasts after a ΔC = −0.1 M shock (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Abrupt changes in endocytic density were followed by a 2–6 min recovery back to the steady-state endocytic density.
source: These abrupt changes in the endocytic density were followed by a 2–6 min recovery back to the steady-state endocytic density, and recovery time depended on the magnitude of the hypotonic shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Recovery time of endocytic density depended on the magnitude of the hypotonic shock.
source: These abrupt changes in the endocytic density were followed by a 2–6 min recovery back to the steady-state endocytic density, and recovery time depended on the magnitude of the hypotonic shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Immediately after the largest shock tested (ΔC = −1.2 M), a similar decrease in the endocytic density was observed for both wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells, 36% and 46%, respectively.
source: Indeed, immediately after the largest shock tested (ΔC = −1.2 M), we observed a similar decrease in the endocytic density for both wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells, 36% and 46%, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Recovery to steady-state endocytic densities occurred in less than 2 min in both wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells after a ΔC = −1.2 M shock.
source: Recovery to steady-state endocytic densities occurred in less than 2 min in both wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells, faster than in protoplasts (Figure 3A, B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The cell wall limits but does not completely cancel the effect of hypotonic shocks on endocytic rates.
source: Our data show that the cell wall limits but does not completely cancel the effect of hypotonic shocks on endocytic rates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of endocytic density changes in walled cells and protoplasts.

claim: The regulation of the endocytic density supplements the regulation performed by the eisosomes to reduce membrane tension.
source: They also suggest that the regulation of the endocytic density supplements the regulation performed by the eisosomes to reduce membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined effects of eisosome disassembly and endocytic density changes.

claim: For all concentrations tested (0–2 M), wild-type cells maintained roughly the same endocytic density.
source: For all concentrations tested (0–2 M), wild-type cells maintained roughly the same endocytic density.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The steady-state endocytic density in pil1Δ cells increased with increasing media osmolarity, up to 56% in 2 M sorbitol.
source: In contrast, the steady-state endocytic density in pil1Δ cells increased with increasing media osmolarity, up to 56% in 2 M sorbitol (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Eisosomes participate in maintaining a constant density of endocytosis independently of the media osmolarity.
source: Our results suggest that eisosomes participate in maintaining a constant density of endocytosis independently of the media osmolarity, not only after an abrupt change in membrane tension, but also when they are at steady state in different osmolarities.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of endocytic density in wild-type and pil1Δ cells at different osmolarities.

claim: Wild-type walled cells at steady state in EMM5S exocytose 4.6% of their plasma membrane surface area per minute.
source: Using this method, we measured that wild-type walled cells at steady state in EMM5S exocytose 4.6% of their plasma membrane surface area per minute (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol, wild-type protoplasts had an exocytosis rate of k0-5=4.4 ± 0.2% min−1.
source: At steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol (Figure 4F and H), wild-type protoplasts had an exocytosis rate similar to walled cells in EMM5S in 0 M sorbitol (k0-5=4.4 ± 0.2% min−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and 4H.

claim: After a ΔC = −0.2 M shock, the exocytosis rate of wild-type protoplasts increased by 41% (k0-5=6.2 ± 0.4% min−1).
source: After a ΔC = −0.2 M shock, the exocytosis rate increased by 41% (k0-5=6.2 ± 0.4% min−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and 4H.

claim: At steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol, the exocytosis rate of pil1Δ protoplasts was k0-5=6.2 ± 0.4% min−1.
source: At steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol (Figure 4G and H), the exocytosis rate of pil1Δ protoplasts was higher than that for walled cells in 0 M sorbitol (k0-5=6.2 ± 0.4% min−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: After a ΔC = −0.05 M shock, the exocytosis rate of pil1Δ protoplasts increased modestly (k0-5=6.8 ± 0.5% min−1).
source: After a ΔC = −0.05 M shock, the exocytosis rate increased modestly (k0-5=6.8 ± 0.5% min−1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: In both wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts, an acute hypotonic shock leads to an increased exocytosis rate.
source: Therefore, in both wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts, an acute hypotonic shock leads to an increased exocytosis rate, which increases surface area and likely reduces membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, 4G, and 4H.

claim: The exocytosis rate of wild-type walled cells at steady state in 1.2 M sorbitol (k0-5=3.1 ± 0.1 % min−1) was 35% smaller than in 0 M sorbitol (k0-5=4.8 ± 0.1 % min−1).
source: The exocytosis rate of wild-type walled cells at steady state in 1.2 M sorbitol (k0-5=3.1 ± 0.1 % min−1, Figure 4C and E) was 35% smaller than in 0 M sorbitol (k0-5=4.8 ± 0.1 % min−1, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and 4E.

claim: In pil1Δ walled cells, the exocytosis rate in 1.2 M sorbitol was only slightly smaller than wild-type cells in the same conditions (k0-5=2.6 ± 0.1% min−1).
source: In addition, in pil1Δ walled cells, the exocytosis rate of walled cells lacking eisosomes in 1.2 M sorbitol was only slightly smaller than wild-type cells in the same conditions (k0-5=2.6 ± 0.1% min−1, Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: After hypotonic shocks, the change in exocytosis rate in walled cells was very limited.
source: After hypotonic shocks, the change in exocytosis rate in walled cells was very limited (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C, 4D, and 4E.

claim: A hypotonic shock of ΔC = −1.2 M did not significantly increase the exocytosis rate of wild-type or pil1Δ walled cells.
source: In fact, our strongest hypotonic shock of ΔC = −1.2 M did not significantly increase the exocytosis rate of wild-type or pil1Δ walled cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Eisosomes are involved in the regulation of the exocytosis rate.
source: In addition, they also demonstrate that eisosomes are involved in the regulation of the exocytosis rate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of exocytosis rates in wild-type and pil1Δ cells.

claim: Blocking exocytosis with BFA increased the death rate of protoplasts after hypotonic shocks.
source: Blocking exocytosis with BFA increased the death rate of protoplasts after hypotonic shocks, confirming our hypothesis (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Blocking actin assembly with LatA made the protoplasts more resistant starting 4 min after the hypotonic shock.
source: Blocking actin assembly, and therefore endocytosis, with LatA made the protoplasts more resistant starting 4 min after the hypotonic shock, also confirming our hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: LatA treatment made the protoplasts less resistant to shock in the initial 2 min after the hypotonic shock.
source: Note that LatA treatment made the protoplasts less resistant to shock in the initial 2 min after the hypotonic shock, which seems in contradiction with our hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For all tested osmolarities at steady state in walled wild-type cells, there was no significant difference in the dynamics of fimbrin recruitment or disassembly, maximum molecule number, or endocytic patch movements.
source: For all tested osmolarities at steady state in walled wild-type cells, we observed no significant difference in the dynamics of fimbrin recruitment or disassembly, maximum molecule number, or endocytic patch movements (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Wild-type walled cells have adaptation mechanisms for chronic exposure to a wide range of osmolarities, which allow them to perform CME in a highly reproducible manner.
source: Our results indicate that wild-type walled cells have adaptation mechanisms for chronic exposure to a wide range of osmolarities, which allow them to perform CME in a highly reproducible manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that fimbrin dynamics are similar across different osmolarities.

claim: Despite a high hypotonic shock of ΔC = −1.2 M, CME proceeded quite similarly to steady-state conditions in wild-type walled cells.
source: Despite the high hypotonic shock, which represents a ~3 MPa drop in pressure, CME proceeded quite similarly to steady-state conditions (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplements 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The maximum number of fimbrin proteins was the same before and after a ΔC = −1.2 M hypotonic shock in wild-type walled cells.
source: The maximum number of fimbrin proteins was the same before and after the hypotonic shock, but fimbrin assembly and disassembly were ~15% faster after the shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Fimbrin assembly and disassembly were approximately 15% faster after a ΔC = −1.2 M hypotonic shock in wild-type walled cells.
source: The maximum number of fimbrin proteins was the same before and after the hypotonic shock, but fimbrin assembly and disassembly were ~15% faster after the shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Dynamics of Fim1p during CME for wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells at steady state in media free of sorbitol was identical.
source: Dynamics of Fim1p during CME for wild-type and pil1Δ walled cells at steady state in media free of sorbitol was identical (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At steady state in media with high sorbitol concentrations, cells lacking eisosomes recruited slightly fewer fimbrin molecules to endocytic patches than wild-type cells.
source: However, at steady state in media with high sorbitol concentrations, cells lacking eisosomes recruited slightly fewer fimbrin molecules to endocytic patches than wild-type cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The maximum number of Fim1p assembled at CME sites in pil1Δ cells in buffers containing 0.8 and 1.2 M sorbitol was 10 and 17% lower, respectively, than in wild-type cells.
source: The maximum number of Fim1p assembled at CME sites in pil1Δ cells in buffers containing 0.8 and 1.2 M sorbitol was 10 and 17% lower, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Within the first 2 min of an acute hypotonic shock from 1.2 M sorbitol to 0 M (ΔC = −1.2 M), the maximum number of Fim1p in pil1Δ cells increased by 30%.
source: Within the first 2 min of an acute hypotonic shock from 1.2 M sorbitol to 0 M (ΔC = −1.2 M), the maximum number of Fim1p increased by 30%, while its timing was shortened by ~30% compared to steady state (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Within the first 2 min of an acute hypotonic shock from 1.2 M sorbitol to 0 M (ΔC = −1.2 M), the timing of Fim1p in pil1Δ cells was shortened by approximately 30% compared to steady state.
source: Within the first 2 min of an acute hypotonic shock from 1.2 M sorbitol to 0 M (ΔC = −1.2 M), the maximum number of Fim1p increased by 30%, while its timing was shortened by ~30% compared to steady state (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Four minutes after a ΔC = −1.2 M hypotonic shock, the dynamics of fimbrin in pil1Δ cells stabilized at its steady-state dynamics in 0 M sorbitol.
source: Four minutes after the hypotonic shock, the dynamics of fimbrin stabilized at its steady-state dynamics in 0 M sorbitol (Figure 6E and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and 6H.

claim: The endocytic actin machinery in cells lacking eisosomes is more sensitive to acute and chronic changes in media osmolarity than in wild-type cells.
source: Overall, our data show that the endocytic actin machinery in cells lacking eisosomes is more sensitive to acute and chronic changes in media osmolarity than in wild-type cells, consistent with a role for eisosome in regulating membrane tension at endocytic sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of fimbrin dynamics in wild-type and pil1Δ cells under different conditions.

claim: Endocytosis in wild-type protoplasts at steady state in a medium containing 0.4 or 0.8 M sorbitol was able to proceed normally by recruiting almost the same number of fimbrin molecules as in walled cells, but with a slightly longer timing.
source: Endocytosis in wild-type protoplasts at steady state in a medium containing 0.4 or 0.8 M sorbitol was able to proceed normally by recruiting almost the same number of fimbrin molecules as in walled cells, but with a slightly longer timing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In a medium with 1.2 M sorbitol, the timing of fimbrin recruitment in wild-type protoplasts was dramatically longer, and endocytosis failed to proceed normally.
source: In contrast, in a medium with 1.2 M sorbitol, the timing of fimbrin recruitment was dramatically longer, and endocytosis failed to proceed normally, as reported by the virtually null speed of patches during the entire time fimbrin was present at the endocytic site (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 0.25 M sorbitol, both wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts were able to perform endocytosis but required a larger amount of Fim1p.
source: At 0.25 M sorbitol, both wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts were able to perform endocytosis but required a larger amount of Fim1p (Figure 7—figure supplements 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 1B and 1C.

claim: During CME, the actin machinery is able to adapt to mechanical cues by mechanisms that are independent of the cell wall.
source: This result indicates that during CME, the actin machinery is able to adapt to mechanical cues by mechanisms that are independent of the cell wall.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that protoplasts can perform endocytosis under high membrane tension.

claim: For both wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts in 0.4 M sorbitol, the temporal evolution of the number of fimbrin molecules and the speed of patches were close to the same metrics measured in walled cells in media without sorbitol.
source: For both wild-type and pil1Δ protoplasts in 0.4 M sorbitol, the temporal evolution of the number of fimbrin molecules and the speed of patches were close to the same metrics measured in walled cells in media without sorbitol (Figure 7—figure supplements 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 1B and 1C.

claim: The osmotic pressure at 0.4 M sorbitol, which is equivalent to a pressure of 1 MPa, is close to the naturally maintained turgor pressure of walled fission yeast cells.
source: These results suggest that the osmotic pressure at these concentrations, which is equivalent to a pressure of 1 MPa, is close to the naturally maintained turgor pressure of walled fission yeast cells, in good agreement with previous measurements (Minc et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of endocytic dynamics in protoplasts at 0.4 M sorbitol and walled cells, and is supported by a citation to previous measurements.

claim: After low (ΔC = −0.05 M) and medium (ΔC = −0.1 M) acute shocks in wild-type protoplasts, no stalled endocytic events were observed.
source: After low (ΔC = −0.05 M) and medium (ΔC = −0.1 M) acute shocks in wild-type protoplasts, we did not observe any stalled endocytic events – when cells started the recruitment of the actin machinery, endocytosis proceeded to successful completion (Figure 7A–C and Figure 7—figure supplements 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A, 7B, 7C, and Figure 7—figure supplements 5.

claim: Two minutes after a ΔC = −0.2 M shock in wild-type protoplasts, endocytic sites recruited 20% more fimbrin, and it took approximately 25% longer to perform endocytosis.
source: In contrast, 2 min after a ΔC = −0.2 M shock, endocytic sites recruited 20% more fimbrin, and it took ~25% longer to perform endocytosis (Figures 7C,D and Figure 7—figure supplements 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C, 7D, and Figure 7—figure supplements 5.

claim: The actin machinery restored its steady-state behavior less than 4 min after a ΔC = −0.2 M shock in wild-type protoplasts.
source: The actin machinery restored its steady-state behavior less than 4 min after the shock (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Two minutes after a ΔC = −0.1 M hypotonic shock, endocytic sites in wild-type protoplasts at steady state in 0.25 M sorbitol accumulated 73% more fimbrin and took approximately 60% longer.
source: Two minutes after the shock, endocytic sites accumulated 73% more fimbrin and took ~60% longer (Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 7A.

claim: The behavior of fimbrin in wild-type protoplasts at steady state in 0.25 M sorbitol after a ΔC = −0.1 M shock was nearly identical to fimbrin dynamics in pil1Δ protoplasts under the same conditions.
source: This behavior was nearly identical to fimbrin dynamics in pil1Δ protoplasts under the same conditions (Figure 7I and Figure 7—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7I and Figure 7—figure supplement 7B.

claim: The endocytic actin machinery adapts to compensate the increase in membrane tension.
source: Altogether, these experiments demonstrate that (a) the endocytic actin machinery adapts to compensate the increase in membrane tension and (b) actin dynamics restores its steady-state behavior within a few minutes, providing the protoplasts survived the hypotonic shock.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations of fimbrin dynamics after hypotonic shocks.

claim: Actin dynamics restores its steady-state behavior within a few minutes after a hypotonic shock, providing the protoplasts survived the hypotonic shock.
source: Altogether, these experiments demonstrate that (a) the endocytic actin machinery adapts to compensate the increase in membrane tension and (b) actin dynamics restores its steady-state behavior within a few minutes, providing the protoplasts survived the hypotonic shock.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations of fimbrin dynamics after hypotonic shocks.

claim: The regulation of membrane tension in hypotonic environment is performed via a combination of at least three mechanisms: the mechanical protection by the cell wall, the disassembly of eisosomes, and the temporary shift in the balance between endocytosis and exocytosis.
source: Our results demonstrate that the regulation of membrane tension in hypotonic environment is performed via a combination of at least three mechanisms: the mechanical protection by the cell wall, the disassembly of eisosomes, and the temporary shift in the balance between endocytosis and exocytosis (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: All three mechanisms (cell wall, eisosome disassembly, and endocytosis/exocytosis balance) are used in parallel.
source: Our data indicate that all three mechanisms are used in parallel since wild-type walled cells are less sensitive to acute hypotonic shocks than wild-type protoplasts and pil1Δ walled cells, and they experience a temporary decrease in their endocytic density for about 2 min after the shock.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of responses in different cell types.

claim: The cell wall provides the largest protection during chronic and acute hypotonic shocks.
source: The cell wall provides the largest protection during chronic and acute hypotonic shocks.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of walled cells and protoplasts.

claim: Removal of the cell wall dramatically affects actin dynamics at endocytic sites and eisosome assembly at the plasma membrane.
source: Removal of the cell wall dramatically affects actin dynamics at endocytic sites and eisosome assembly at the plasma membrane (Figures 1B, C and 7 – Supplement 1B and 7 – Supplement 1C), and greatly increased the effect of hypotonic shocks on exocytosis (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Endocytosis in protoplasts still proceeds in media with osmolarity as low as 0.25 M, where a large fraction of eisosomes is disassembled.
source: It is surprising that endocytosis in protoplasts still proceeds in media with osmolarity as low as 0.25 M, where a large fraction of eisosomes is disassembled.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing endocytosis in protoplasts at 0.25 M sorbitol.

claim: The actin endocytic machinery can overcome membrane tensions high enough to rupture the plasma membrane.
source: In fact, the actin endocytic machinery can overcome membrane tensions high enough to rupture the plasma membrane since we did not see stalled actin patches, or actin comet tails, in any of our experiments.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of stalled actin patches or comet tails in the experiments.

claim: The results contrast with recent data in S. cerevisiae where endocytosis is blocked and actin comet tails are formed within 2 min of a hypotonic shock.
source: Our results contrast with recent data in S. cerevisiae (Riggi et al., 2019) where endocytosis is blocked and actin comet tails are formed within 2 min of a hypotonic shock.
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with previous work in a different yeast species.

claim: These differences may highlight species specificities.
source: These differences may highlight species specificities.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the interpretation of differences between species.

claim: Eisosomes play a critical role in the regulation of membrane tension and membrane integrity through dynamic remodeling and scaffolding of the plasma membrane.
source: Our results add to a growing body of evidence that eisosomes play a critical role in the regulation of membrane tension and membrane integrity through dynamic remodeling and scaffolding of the plasma membrane (Kabeche et al., 2015; Moseley, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and citations to previous work.

claim: Membrane tension is decreased via the disassembly of eisosomes, through release of excess membrane surface area.
source: Therefore, our data indicate that membrane tension is decreased via the disassembly of eisosomes, through release of excess membrane surface area.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the micropipette aspiration experiments and eisosome disassembly data.

claim: At steady state, Pil1p undergoes rapid exchange at the eisosome ends.
source: Single-molecule imaging in our lab demonstrated that at steady state, Pil1p undergoes rapid exchange at the eisosome ends (Lacy et al., 2017), potentially providing a convenient route for rapid eisosome disassembly, analogous to filament depolymerization, in combination with eisosome breaking.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work from the same lab.

claim: Disassembled eisosome components have altered phosphorylation level or sub-cellular localization.
source: Disassembled eisosome components have altered phosphorylation level or sub-cellular localization, which potentially relays the signaling from eisosome integrity to endocytosis and/or exocytosis (Riggi et al., 2018; Walther et al., 2007), possibly via TORC2 (Riggi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cells endocytose about 2% of their surface area per minute through CME.
source: Using our data, we estimate that cells endocytose about 2% of their surface area per minute through CME, confirming our previous measurements (Berro and Pollard, 2014a; Berro and Pollard, 2014b).
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from the current data and is consistent with previous measurements.

claim: In pil1Δ protoplasts initially at steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol, the net surface area added over 10 min after a ΔC = −0.05 M shock by reduction in endocytosis and increase in exocytosis corresponds to an 11% increase in the protoplast surface area.
source: For example, in pil1Δ protoplasts, initially at steady state in 0.4 M sorbitol, the endocytosis rate is reduced by ~25% for ~10 min after an acute hypotonic shock of ΔC = −0.05 M, while the exocytosis rate increased by ~10%. The net surface area added over that period by reduction in endocytosis and increase in exocytosis corresponds to a 5% + 6% = 11% increase in the protoplast surface area, close to the ~12% surface area increase we measured.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations from the measured endocytosis and exocytosis rates.

claim: Modulating the endocytosis and exocytosis rates is an efficient way to increase the surface area of the plasma membrane by large amounts, but this process is relatively slow compared to eisosome disassembly.
source: These estimates demonstrate that modulating the endocytosis and exocytosis rates is an efficient way to increase the surface area of the plasma membrane by large amounts, but this process is relatively slow compared to eisosome disassembly.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of time scales for different membrane tension regulation mechanisms.

claim: Fission yeast CME is very robust and can proceed in a wide range of osmolarities and membrane tensions.
source: Our data demonstrate that fission yeast CME is very robust and can proceed in a wide range of osmolarities and membrane tensions.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Even cells devoid of a cell wall and eisosomes were able to perform endocytosis after an acute change in membrane tension, as long as their plasma membrane was not damaged and cells remained alive.
source: Even cells devoid of a cell wall and eisosomes were able to perform endocytosis after an acute change in membrane tension, as long as their plasma membrane was not damaged and cells remained alive.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing endocytosis in pil1Δ protoplasts after hypotonic shocks.

claim: Under conditions where membrane tension and turgor pressure were significantly increased, the endocytic actin machinery took longer and assembled a larger number of fimbrin molecules to successfully produce endocytic vesicles.
source: Under conditions where membrane tension and turgor pressure were significantly increased, we observed that the endocytic actin machinery took longer and assembled a larger number of fimbrin molecules to successfully produce endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing changes in fimbrin dynamics under high membrane tension.

claim: This result strongly supports the idea that the actin machinery provides the force that counteracts membrane tension and turgor pressure and deforms the plasma membrane into an endocytic pit.
source: This result strongly supports the idea that the actin machinery provides the force that counteracts membrane tension and turgor pressure and deforms the plasma membrane into an endocytic pit.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the data showing increased actin assembly under high membrane tension.

claim: Actin dynamics is controlled via a mechanical or geometrical regulation, where actin assembles until the plasma membrane is deformed and pinched off.
source: Our data suggest that actin dynamics is controlled via a mechanical or geometrical regulation, where actin assembles until the plasma membrane is deformed and pinched off.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The activity and/or recruitment of proteins upstream of the actin nucleators may be enhanced by increased membrane tension.
source: An alternative, and non-mutually exclusive, hypothesis is that the activity and/or recruitment of proteins upstream of the actin nucleators may be enhanced by increased membrane tension.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the molecular mechanism.

claim: The decrease in the number of endocytic events after an increase in membrane tension leads to an increase in the concentration of endocytic proteins in the cytoplasm, which can then enhance the reactions performed at the endocytic sites.
source: A third hypothesis is that the decrease in the number of endocytic events after an increase in membrane tension leads to an increase in the concentration of endocytic proteins in the cytoplasm, which can then enhance the reactions performed at the endocytic sites.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the molecular mechanism.

claim: 65–85% of the total cellular content of key proteins involved in the endocytic actin machinery is localized to endocytic sites at any time.
source: Sirotkin et al., 2010 measured that 65–85% of the total cellular content of key proteins involved in the endocytic actin machinery is localized to endocytic sites at any time.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: One or several early endocytic proteins are sensitive to membrane tension, and they either fail to bind the plasma membrane or prevent the triggering of actin assembly when membrane tension is high.
source: However, it is more likely that one or several early endocytic proteins are sensitive to membrane tension, and they either fail to bind the plasma membrane or prevent the triggering of actin assembly when membrane tension is high.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the molecular mechanism.

claim: The proportion of stalled clathrin-coated pits increases when membrane tension increases in mammalian cells.
source: This idea would be consistent with results from mammalian cells demonstrating that the proportion of stalled clathrin-coated pits increases when membrane tension increases (Ferguson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work in mammalian cells.

claim: Several endocytic proteins that arrive before or concomitantly with the activators of the actin machinery contain BAR domains.
source: In addition, several endocytic proteins that arrive before or concomitantly with the activators of the actin machinery contain BAR domains (such as Syp1p, Bzz1p, and Cdc15p), and other members of this domain family (which also includes Pil1p) have been shown to bind membranes in a tension-sensitive manner.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about protein domains and their properties.

claim: The results are expected to be relevant to the study of CME and membrane tension regulation in other eukaryotes since the molecular machineries for endocytosis, exocytosis, and osmotic response are highly conserved.
source: We expect our results to be relevant to the study of CME and membrane tension regulation in other eukaryotes since the molecular machineries for endocytosis, exocytosis, and osmotic response are highly conserved.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Regulation of membrane tension and CME are particularly critical during cell polarization.
source: In addition, regulation of membrane tension and CME are particularly critical during cell polarization (Mostov et al., 2000), during neuron development and shape changes (Urbina et al., 2018), and at synapses where large pools of membranes are added and retrieved on a very fast time scale (Nicholson-Fish et al., 2016; Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Regulation of membrane tension and CME are particularly critical during neuron development and shape changes.
source: In addition, regulation of membrane tension and CME are particularly critical during cell polarization (Mostov et al., 2000), during neuron development and shape changes (Urbina et al., 2018), and at synapses where large pools of membranes are added and retrieved on a very fast time scale (Nicholson-Fish et al., 2016; Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Regulation of membrane tension and CME are particularly critical at synapses where large pools of membranes are added and retrieved on a very fast time scale.
source: In addition, regulation of membrane tension and CME are particularly critical during cell polarization (Mostov et al., 2000), during neuron development and shape changes (Urbina et al., 2018), and at synapses where large pools of membranes are added and retrieved on a very fast time scale (Nicholson-Fish et al., 2016; Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.
